pr_title: shutdown: check whether the DM mapping table exists before fsync fix systemd-shutdown hang all the time
pr_comments:
> Hmm, isn't this a kernel bug if a sync() on DM devices that have no targets associated with them hangs?
> 
> @oniko @mbroz does this look right to you?
> 
> (background: this is the final shutdown code, where we robustly detach all remaining loopback, MD, and DM devices. And sync before.)


there is a dead loop in this case, kernel will defer process io if map is null, kernel don't drop this io, it's right because dm device will resume soon, but reboot cause device never resume and enter shutdown.

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a4b80de9-c580-44b5-9cba-81d0774dd6de)

> Hmm, isn't this a kernel bug if a sync() on DM devices that have no targets associated with them hangs?

I'm not sure, but I expect it to be intentional.

But if you want to tear down the device unconditionally and fast, we often use a strategy to force reload device-mapper table with the error target, this will quickly kill all users (all operations fail over this device ), and the target can be removed then (or can be ignored, as it points to no real devices). (Cryptsetup used this if someone tried to access a legacy internal keyslot mapped device.)

I'm not sure if this helps; just FYI.

So  'DM device without' target table line likely doesn't exist - as it cannot be resumed/opened/synced.
But I guess the idea here is about  i.e.  'linear'  DM device that is referring some 'lost'  iscsi device or something that basically  'blocks'  any IO on this linear device - until there is something where this IO can be routed to.
This is surely NOT a bug -  it's the user/admin responsibility to  'fix' the table line and select i.e.  new destination device -  or  as  mbroz  pointed out   such  'linear'  target can be replaced  with  'error' or  'zero'  target according the needs (errroring or  silencing all dumped IO there)

So whoever is doing a 'shutting' down sequence - should be killing thing in some 'top->down' manner a replacing things in a way to cause  'the least' damage to user's data   (i.e.  device composed from multiple devices where only one is being lost...)

The most radical can be of course   'dmsetup remove_all --force'  which is doing this 'error' target replacement -
so with repeated invoke & umount - this should eventually succeed  - unless it deadlocks somewhere in the kernel's filesystem code which cannot  cope with  'error' device well...

For DM remove - we do require open count of a device  ==  0   - this should be almost always achievable - unless there is a kernel bug -  such bug should be reported with reproducer.

> I'm not sure, but I expect it to be intentional.
> 
> But if you want to tear down the device unconditionally and fast, we often use a strategy to force reload device-mapper table with the error target, this will quickly kill all users (all operations fail over this device ), and the target can be removed then (or can be ignored, as it points to no real devices). (Cryptsetup used this if someone tried to access a legacy internal keyslot mapped device.)

We want to tear down the device "reasonably quickly" here, without losing data. hence, we typically do sync() things here.

This is the 2nd phase of shutdown after all, i.e. it just cleans up what the "clean" phase of the shutdown didn't manage to clean up, as a safety net if you so will.

Hence, I think something that "quickly kills all users" is not really what we want here. We are fine if the syncing takes a bit of time, but otoh does remain within bounds.

> So whoever is doing a 'shutting' down sequence - should be killing thing in some 'top->down' manner a replacing things in a way to cause 'the least' damage to user's data (i.e. device composed from multiple devices where only one is being lost...)

So, this here is the 2nd phase of shutdown as mentioned, it kills/detaches everything not covered by the clean phase. At this point we just kill/umount/sync/detach in a tight loop until nothings changes anymore. This intentionally does *not* respect dependencies between things anymore. In a correct world it wouldn't do anything at all anymore. 

This all is different from the 1st phase of shutdown stops all services respecting deps and if everything works correctly should make sure everything is shutdown correctly. If everyone wrote their units correctly then the 1st phase should not leave around anything anymore that the 2nd phase would have to clean up. But we don't live in that world.

> The most radical can be of course 'dmsetup remove_all --force' which is doing this 'error' target replacement - so with repeated invoke & umount - this should eventually succeed - unless it deadlocks somewhere in the kernel's filesystem code which cannot cope with 'error' device well...

So, this doesn't look like it is what we want. We want some middle ground: i.e. everything that is in flight should be sync'ed, but we do not insist that everything is entirely clean. Hence normally we just sync() and go on.

Theoretically - lvm2  could implement some  'forcible'  deactivation on its own - likely we have good knowledge about the connection between devices and their importance and so on - however this would be rather long term goal - since this is not exactly trivial task when solved correctly.

> Theoretically - lvm2 could implement some 'forcible' deactivation on its own - likely we have good knowledge about the connection between devices and their importance and so on - however this would be rather long term goal - since this is not exactly trivial task when solved correctly.

systemd does not really provide any hooks into that 2nd phase of shutdown. and I am not fond of the idea of giving people hooks for that tight loop of destruction. I am kinda concerned that people might to stuff there that is "too smart", might depend on external stuff, and so on.

There is always a 'some' solution in form of 'timeout' with forcible unconditional  SysRQ+B.  Question timeout this should be  - as that may heavily depend on some disk speeds and amount of work it needs to be done - so probably not a single number to fits them all -  so maybe monitoring 'disk-io'  can be measured here -  work to the point there is some buggy writing busy-loop somewhere thought.....
My suggesion for a fix is waiting in #34330. PTAL.

issue_context.title: systemd-shutdown hang all the timen (if DM devices with no targets exist)
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

255

### Used distribution

Fedora 39

### Linux kernel version used

kernel-6.6.0-136.x86_64

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

None

### Component

systemd

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

The computer is shut down or restarted.

### Unexpected behaviour you saw

systemd-shutdown hang all the time

### Steps to reproduce the problem

During the shutdown, all DMs are detached. The fsync_path_at() is delivered , and then the ioctl() is executed to delete the DMs. However, the DMs are hanged in the fsync:
```
static int delete_dm(DeviceMapper *m) {
...
        r = fsync_path_at(AT_FDCWD, m->path);
        if (r < 0)
                log_debug_errno(r, "Failed to sync DM block device %s, ignoring: %m", m->path);

        return RET_NERRNO(ioctl(fd, DM_DEV_REMOVE, &(struct dm_ioctl) {
...
}
```
According to the dm device information parsed by the vmcore, the dm has been created successfully, but the mapping table has not been loaded. The I/O delivered by the fsync is delayed. However, the systemd-shutdown process has been started and all processes are stopped,and the mapping table cannot be loaded. As a result, the I/O is suspended, and systemd-shutdown is hanged as well.

In addition to /dev/watchdog(The /dev/watchdog and the /dev/watchdog0 device does not exist on my machine), are there any other methods that can prevent the system from being stuck? ()
Or check whether the DM mapping table exists before fsync()?



### Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue

_No response_
comments:
I prepped an fix in #34330, that should address the issue here. It's entirely generic and puts a global timeout on any kind of fsync() we issue from the shutdown binary. It does not try to be smart in anyway, but that's a good ting, and should mean we won't hang unbounded here.

As I understand this is triggered by a local mishandling of the device. I think it#s hence fine if we handle this via a timeout here. We don't have to try to be "clean" in shutdown.c because the triggering condition isn't clean either.
Aynway, would be great if you could check if #34330 makes the issue go away for you?

> Aynway, would be great if you could check if #34330 makes the issue go away for you?

Thanks. The system can be shutdown within bounded time. Close this issue.
